claims.section: A setting is not a process window
claims.claim: A robust process is characterized by a tested region of acceptable output, not merely one nominal setting combination.
claims.applicability: Process development with measurable acceptance criteria.
claims.exclusions: Does not imply every factor can vary independently.
claims.basis: NIST process/product improvement and experimental-design framework supports studying factor ranges and response behavior rather than relying on one point.

claims.claim: Process-window work requires measurable product/process responses tied to acceptance requirements before input ranges are judged acceptable.
claims.exclusions: Regulated/site quality systems may impose additional response definitions.
claims.basis: NIST experimental methods require defined responses; ISO provides plastics-specific dimensional acceptance context.

claims.claim: Sensitivity should be tested deliberately within safe/material/equipment limits and only the actually tested region should be claimed.
claims.exclusions: Safety-critical or destructive ranges remain prohibited unless governed separately.
claims.basis: Designed experiments support deliberate range testing while ASTM material-specific conditions prevent treating arbitrary extremes as acceptable.

claims.claim: A reproducible process record should identify material, equipment/tool context, key parameters with units and measured part results.
claims.exclusions: Regulated products may require additional records.
claims.basis: ASTM emphasizes consistent moulding-condition reporting and NIST emphasizes traceable experimental conditions/responses.

claims.claim: Parameter names/setpoints should be documented with measurement location, meaning, units and assumptions when cross-machine ambiguity exists.
claims.exclusions: Does not prescribe one schema.
claims.basis: Consistent parameter reporting is supported; explicit cross-controller semantics require machine documentation.

claims.claim: Engineering changes should retain the reason, evidence and resulting measured response so causal claims remain auditable.
claims.exclusions: Emergency safety actions may precede formal analysis.
claims.basis: Statistical experimental practice requires recorded factors/responses and interpretation of evidence.

claims.claim: A cavity-pressure sensor measures pressure closer to where the part forms than an upstream machine injection-pressure signal and can reduce ambiguity from upstream losses.
claims.exclusions: Sensor location and type still affect what is measured.
claims.basis: Manufacturer and peer-reviewed evidence both use cavity pressure as a direct in-mould process signal distinct from machine-side pressure.

claims.claim: Pressure-curve features such as rise, transfer, peak and decay depend on sensor position, calibration, mould geometry and process state.
claims.exclusions: No universal curve threshold is asserted.
claims.basis: Both sources interpret pressure features through sensor/process context rather than universal values.

claims.claim: A pressure-quality correlation can support monitoring within the validated study range but does not prove universal causation outside that range.
claims.applicability: Statistical process monitoring using cavity pressure.
claims.exclusions: Validated causal mechanisms may have stronger evidence.
claims.basis: Kistler describes model/correlation-based quality monitoring while NIST requires statistical interpretations to retain assumptions and scope.

claims.claim: Designed experiments can estimate factor effects and selected interactions more efficiently and defensibly than casual one-factor changes when variables interact.
claims.exclusions: Design choice depends on objectives, constraints and assumptions.
claims.basis: Experimental design is a core NIST handbook topic for process/product improvement.

claims.claim: A DOE should define measurable responses, controllable factors/ranges and nuisance variables before execution.
claims.exclusions: Specific design matrices are not prescribed.
claims.basis: This is foundational experimental-design practice in the NIST handbook.

claims.claim: Statistical significance should be interpreted alongside effect size, measurement adequacy, engineering meaning and physical plausibility before becoming a process rule.
claims.exclusions: Does not reject valid empirical control models.
claims.basis: NIST explicitly frames statistical methods with underlying assumptions, measurement characterization and interpretation.

claims.claim: Capability indices should not substitute for establishing a statistically stable process and credible measurement system.
claims.exclusions: Exact stability tests/index thresholds depend on method/site definition.
claims.basis: NIST separates process characterization from measurement characterization and documents stability/repeatability prerequisites.

claims.section: Separate process variation from measurement variation
claims.claim: Measurement repeatability/reproducibility can materially affect observed variation and must be understood before attributing variation to the moulding process.
claims.exclusions: No generic GRR threshold is asserted.
claims.basis: NIST chapter explicitly covers repeatability, reproducibility, stability and uncertainty.

claims.claim: Capability numbers depend on specification limits, distribution assumptions, sampling and process stability and should be reported with those conditions.
claims.exclusions: Specific industry/customer definitions may impose additional rules.
claims.basis: NIST production-process characterization requires assumptions and data context rather than an isolated index.

claims.claim: Monitoring should favor signals with a defensible relationship to process mechanisms and part quality rather than arbitrary available values.
claims.exclusions: Useful signals vary by process and instrumentation.
claims.basis: Kistler maps cavity/machine signals to quality monitoring; NIST supports mechanism-informed process monitoring.

claims.section: Limits are not merely historical min/max
claims.claim: Alarm/control limits should account for normal variation, measurement behavior, validated process window and consequences rather than copying historical extrema.
claims.exclusions: Product/specification limits are distinct from statistical control limits.
claims.basis: NIST monitoring and measurement characterization distinguish statistical behavior from arbitrary observed ranges.

claims.section: An alarm is a decision aid
claims.claim: A process alarm indicates a defined threshold/event but does not by itself prove product disposition or root cause.
claims.exclusions: A validated quality-prediction system may have approved disposition rules within its validation scope.
claims.basis: Monitoring systems detect deviations; exact disposition logic is application/validation specific.

claims.claim: Post-mould dimensions can change after ejection through continued thermal/material processes, including applicable post-mould shrinkage and moisture effects.
claims.exclusions: Mechanisms and time scales are material-specific.
claims.basis: ISO explicitly defines post-moulding shrinkage and distinguishes moisture uptake; ASTM addresses shrinkage from mould dimensions.

claims.claim: Dimensional comparison requires defined conditioning/time/environment and measurement method so conditioning effects are not mistaken for process changes.
claims.exclusions: Exact conditioning follows product/material standards.
claims.basis: Current plastics tolerance framework and shrinkage standard require controlled dimensional reference conditions.

claims.claim: Cavity pattern, time trend, directionality and controlled process/material comparisons can help distinguish mould, process and material contributions to dimensional variation.
claims.exclusions: These observations do not automatically prove causation.
claims.basis: Sources establish multiple dimensional influences; the proposed discrimination sequence remains an engineering diagnostic framework.

claims.claim: Short fibres develop spatially varying orientation distributions during mould filling, including through-thickness and local-flow effects.
claims.exclusions: Distribution depends on grade, flow and geometry.
claims.basis: X-ray micro-CT study directly measured local fibre distributions and demonstrated flow-region dependence.

claims.claim: Fibre orientation can create directional mechanical and shrinkage behavior and therefore influence warpage/performance.
claims.exclusions: Magnitude requires grade-specific data.
claims.basis: Peer-reviewed sources link fibre orientation with properties and shrinkage/warpage-related defects.

claims.claim: Gate/flow geometry and filling conditions can alter orientation, so generic isotropic shrinkage factors are insufficient for reinforced-part prediction.
claims.exclusions: Validated material models can be used within their calibrated scope.
claims.basis: Study shows local flow type and modelling choices materially alter orientation predictions.

claims.claim: Small flow thickness increases sensitivity to thermal loss and flow resistance during filling.
claims.exclusions: No universal thickness threshold defines thin-wall for all materials/geometries.
claims.basis: General material-specific moulding conditions are supported, but the thin-wall flow claim needs dedicated thin-wall research or manufacturer evidence.

claims.claim: Injection rate, pressure, acceleration/control response and shot-size suitability can constrain thin-wall filling; nominal pressure rating alone does not prove suitability.
claims.exclusions: Capability must be evaluated on the actual machine/material/mould.
claims.basis: Requires current machine-manufacturer or dedicated thin-wall process evidence before verification.

claims.claim: Required filling rate depends on polymer rheology, geometry, gate and thermal condition and must be established within supplier/equipment limits.
claims.exclusions: No universal speed recipe.
claims.basis: ASTM establishes material-specific conditions but dedicated thin-wall evidence is needed for full support.

claims.section: Equal geometry does not guarantee equal filling
claims.claim: Multi-cavity moulds can show cavity-to-cavity differences because local pressure, flow path, thermal and venting conditions need not be identical.
claims.exclusions: Balanced systems may achieve very close cavity behavior.
claims.basis: Peer-reviewed multi-cavity sensor work and industrial monitoring evidence show cavity-specific pressure/process variation.

claims.claim: Cavity-specific fill/pressure/part measurements should be retained because pooled data can hide a biased or unstable cavity.
claims.exclusions: Sampling plans may use validated aggregation after equivalence is established.
claims.basis: Multi-cavity study measures cavities individually; statistical practice supports preserving subgroup structure relevant to variation.

claims.claim: Systematic cavity bias should be distinguished from random cycle variation before tooling/process changes are attributed to imbalance.
claims.exclusions: Does not define a universal balance tolerance.
claims.basis: Experimental cavity-pressure evidence plus statistical variation analysis support this distinction.

claims.section: The label does not define a process
claims.claim: High-performance polymer families differ materially in processing temperature, moisture sensitivity and thermal stability, so the family label alone cannot define a process.
claims.exclusions: Exact properties depend on grade/formulation.
claims.basis: ASTM requires material-specific conditions and BASF families show markedly different processing requirements.

claims.section: Use grade documents as controlling evidence
claims.claim: Current grade-specific supplier processing/TDS/SDS plus equipment compatibility checks control production values rather than generic family recipes.
claims.exclusions: Product qualification/site requirements may be more restrictive.
claims.basis: ASTM explicitly defers to material specifications/supplier guidance when conditions are not prescribed.

claims.claim: For elevated-temperature materials, melt history and residence distribution can be important and generic family setpoints must not replace current supplier requirements.
claims.applicability: High-temperature thermoplastics with supplier thermal/residence limits.
claims.exclusions: No universal thermal margin is asserted.
claims.basis: Manufacturer guide provides material-scoped processing/residence guidance and cautions against inappropriate thermal exposure.

claims.section: Several mechanisms can fit the same symptom
claims.claim: Complex moulding symptoms such as dimensional drift can arise from multiple material, thermal, pressure, cooling, measurement or tooling mechanisms.
claims.exclusions: A sufficiently instrumented case may rule out alternatives.
claims.basis: Current tolerance framework and review literature explicitly identify multiple interacting dimensional/process influences.

claims.claim: Diagnostic measurements/tests should be chosen for their ability to produce different expected outcomes for competing hypotheses.
claims.exclusions: Does not prescribe one DOE or instrument set.
claims.basis: Experimental design and model discrimination principles support selecting informative controlled comparisons.

claims.claim: When available evidence cannot distinguish plausible causes, the unresolved alternatives should be documented rather than declaring an unsupported root cause.
claims.exclusions: Later evidence can resolve the hold.
claims.basis: Statistical inference requires assumptions/uncertainty to remain visible; this is also an explicit MouldMaster accuracy policy.

summary.rule: No chapter is promoted by this audit; thin-wall machine-capability wording remains held pending controlling evidence.
